'''''Prunus mume''''', also known as a '''Chinese plum''',<ref name=IUCN/><ref name=EOL>{{Cite EOL |id=628584 |title=''Prunus mume'' (Sieb.) Sieb. & Zucc. |access-date=3 April 2025}} [https://web.archive.org/web/20241127170826/https://eol.org/pages/628584 Archived] from the original on 27 November 2024.</ref> is a tree species in the family [[Rosaceae]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Zhang |first1=Qixiang |last2=Chen |first2=Wenbin |last3=Sun |first3=Lidan |last4=Zhao |first4=Fangying |last5=Huang |first5=Bangqing |last6=Yang |first6=Weiru |last7=Tao |first7=Ye |last8=Wang |first8=Jia |last9=Yuan |first9=Zhiqiong |last10=Fan |first10=Guangyi |last11=Xing |first11=Zhen |last12=Han |first12=Changlei |last13=Pan |first13=Huitang |last14=Zhong |first14=Xiao |last15=Shi |first15=Wenfang |date=2012-12-27 |title=The genome of Prunus mume |journal=Nature Communications |language=en |volume=3 |issue=1 |page=1318 |doi=10.1038/ncomms2290  |doi-access=free|issn=2041-1723 |pmc=3535359 |pmid=23271652|bibcode=2012NatCo...3.1318Z }}</ref> It is also referenced by its flowers as '''plum blossom'''.<ref>{{cite book |last=Fan |first=Chengda |title=Treatises of the Supervisor and Guardian of the Cinnamon Sea |publisher=University of Washington Press |year=2010 |isbn=978-0-295-99079-8 |edition=Translated |location=[[Seattle]] |page=LV}}</ref> Although referred to as a ''plum'' in English, it is classified in the ''Armeniaca'' section of the [[genus]] ''[[Prunus]]'', making it an [[apricot]]. ''Mei'' flowers, or ''meihua'' ({{lang|zh|梅花}}), which bloom in the late winter and early spring, notably during the [[Chinese New Year|spring festival]] (春節), symbolize endurance, as they are the first to bloom despite the cold; the flower is one of the [[Three Friends of Winter]].

The plant is intimately associated with art, literature, and everyday life in China,<ref>{{Cite book |title=The garden plants of China |date=1999 |publisher=Timber Press |isbn=978-0-88192-470-1 |editor-last=Valder |editor-first=Peter |location=Portland, Or}}</ref> from where it was then introduced to Korea, Vietnam, and Japan. In [[East Asian cuisine]] ([[Chinese cuisine|Chinese]], [[Japanese cuisine|Japanese]], [[Korean cuisine|Korean]], and [[Vietnamese cuisine]]), the fruit, known as ''meizi'' ([[wikt:梅子|梅子]]) in Chinese, is used in juices and sauces; as a flavoring for alcohol; and may be [[Umeboshi|pickled]] or [[Li hing mui|dried]]. It is also used in [[traditional Chinese medicine]]. ''Meihua'' are also appreciated for their characteristic fragrance, which is unique among apricots.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ding |first1=Anqi |last2=Bao |first2=Fei |last3=Ding |first3=Aiqin |last4=Zhang |first4=Qixiang |date=December 2022 |title=Cold Hardiness of Prunus mume 'Xiang Ruibai' and Its Parents Based on Biological Indexes and Physical Parameters |journal=Forests |language=en |volume=13 |issue=12 |page=2163 |doi=10.3390/f13122163 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2022Fore...13.2163D |issn=1999-4907}}</ref> 

''Prunus mume'' should not be confused with the plum ''[[Prunus salicina]]'', a related species also grown in China, Japan, Korea, and Vietnam also referred to with the common name of Chinese plum, nor with the common apricot ''[[Prunus armeniaca]]'', which is closely related under the same section.

== Origin ==
''Prunus mume'' originated in the region around the [[Yangtze River]] in southern China and was cultivated domestically for both its ornamental beauty and its fruit.<ref name=uem>{{cite journal|title=Phylogenetic relationships in the stone fruit group of ''Prunus'' as revealed by restriction fragment analysis of chloroplast DNA|journal=The Japanese Journal of Genetics|volume=66|year=1991|issue=1|page=60|quote=''P. mume'' had its origin in South China around the Yangtze River (Kyotani, 1989b).|first1=Chiyomi|last1=Uematsu|first2=Tetsuo|last2=Sasakuma|first3=Yasunari|last3=Ogihara|doi=10.1266/jjg.66.59|pmid=1676591|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Yü |first=Ying-shih |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mb-lDAAAQBAJ&q=Chinese+History+and+Culture%3A+Sixth+Century+B.C.E.+to+Seventeenth+Century+Get+access++Ying-shih+Y%C3%BC |title=Chinese History and Culture: Sixth Century B.C.E. to Seventeenth Century, Volume 1 |date=2016-09-20 |publisher=Columbia University Press |isbn=978-0-231-54201-2 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bao |first1=Fei |last2=Ding |first2=Anqi |last3=Zhang |first3=Tengxun |last4=Luo |first4=Le |last5=Wang |first5=Jia |last6=Cheng |first6=Tangren |last7=Zhang |first7=Qixiang |date=2019-02-01 |title=Expansion of PmBEAT genes in the Prunus mume genome induces characteristic floral scent production |journal=Horticulture Research |volume=6 |issue=1 |page=24 |doi=10.1038/s41438-018-0104-4 |issn=2052-7276 |pmc=6355818 |pmid=30729014|bibcode=2019HorR....6...24B }}</ref> It was later introduced to [[Japan]],<ref name=fang>{{cite journal|last=Fang|first=J|author2=Twito, T |author3=Zhang, Z |author4= Chao, CT |title=Genetic relationships among fruiting-mei (Prunus mume Sieb. et Zucc.) cultivars evaluated with AFLP and SNP markers.|journal=Genome|date=October It can be found in sparse forests, stream sides, forested slopes along trails, and mountains, sometimes at altitudes up to {{cvt|1700|-|3100|m}}, and regions of cultivation.<ref name=eflora/>

== Description ==
''Prunus mume'' is a [[deciduous]] tree that starts to flower in mid-winter, typically around January until late February in [[East Asia]]. It can grow to {{cvt|4|–|10|m}} tall.<ref name=eflora/> The flowers are {{cvt|2|–|2.5|cm}} in diameter and have a strong fragrant scent.<ref name=eflora>{{cite web|title=Armeniaca mume in Flora of China|url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200010631|publisher=Missouri Botanical Garden (St. Louis, MO) & Harvard University Herbaria (Cambridge, MA)|work=eFloras|access-date=21 August 2011}}</ref> They have colors in varying shades of white, pink, and red.<ref>{{cite web|last=Wessel|first=Mark|title=Prunus mume: A bridge between winter and spring.|url=http://wesselsgardenway.com/2011/03/24/prunus-mume-a-bridge-between-winter-and-spring/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120331014046/http://wesselsgardenway.com/2011/03/24/prunus-mume-a-bridge-between-winter-and-spring/|archive-date=March 31, 2012|access-date=21 August 2011}}</ref> The leaves appear shortly after the petals fall, are oval-shaped with a pointed tip, and are 4–8 cm long and 2.5–5 cm wide.<ref name=eflora/> The fruit ripens in early summer, around June and July in East Asia, and coincides with the [[East Asian rainy season]], the ''[[meiyu]]'' ([[wikt:梅雨|梅雨]], "plum rain").<ref>{{cite book|last=Herbert Edgar|first=Wright|title=Global climates since the last glacial maximum|year=1993|publisher=University of Minnesota Press|location=Minneapolis|isbn=978-0-8166-2145-3|page=251|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=c93dGzg8vM8C}}</ref> The [[drupe]] is {{cvt|2|–|3|cm}} in diameter with a groove running from the stalk to the tip.<ref name=eflora/> The skin turns yellow, sometimes with a red blush, as it ripens, and the flesh becomes yellow. The tree is [[Agriculture|cultivate]]d for its [[fruit]] and [[flower]]s.<ref name="RBGKew">{{cite web |title=''Prunus mume'' (mume) |url=http://www.kew.org/plants-fungi/Prunus-mume.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111109224525/http://www.kew.org/plants-fungi/Prunus-mume.htm |archive-date=November 9, 2011 |access-date=August 9, 2011 |publisher=[[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web | url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/prunus-mume/ |title = Prunus mume (Japanese Apricot) | North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox}}</ref>

== Names ==
Native to southern China, where it is known as ''mei'' (梅).<ref name="eflora" /><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Zhang |first1=Qixiang |last2=Zhang |first2=He |last3=Sun |first3=Lidan |last4=Fan |first4=Guangyi |last5=Ye |first5=Meixia |last6=Jiang |first6=Libo |last7=Liu |first7=Xin |last8=Ma |first8=Kaifeng |last9=Shi |first9=Chengcheng |last10=Bao |first10=Fei |last11=Guan |first11=Rui |last12=Han |first12=Yu |last13=Fu |first13=Yuanyuan |last14=Pan |first14=Huitang |last15=Chen |first15=Zhaozhe |date=27 April 2018 |title=The genetic architecture of floral traits in the woody plant Prunus mume |journal=Nature Communications |volume=9 |issue=1 |page=1702 |bibcode=2018NatCo...9.1702Z |doi=10.1038/s41467-018-04093-z  |doi-access=free|pmc=5923208 |pmid=29703940 |quote=Mei (''Prunus mume'') is an ornamental woody plant that has been domesticated in East Asia for thousands of years. |last16=Li |first16=Liangwei |last17=Wang |first17=Jia |last18=Lv |first18=Meiqi |last19=Zheng |first19=Tangchun |last20=Yuan |first20=Cunquan |last21=Zhou |first21=Yuzhen |last22=Lee |first22=Simon Ming-Yuen |last23=Yan |first23=Xiaolan |last24=Xu |first24=Xun |last25=Wu |first25=Rongling |last26=Chen |first26=Wenbin |last27=Cheng |first27=Tangren}}</ref> The scientific name combines the Latin [[wikt:prunus|''prūnus'']] ("[[Prunus domestica|(European) plum tree]]") and the obsolete Japanese pronunciation of 梅 (''mume''), which is ultimately likely derived from [[Middle Chinese]]. The plant is known by a number of different names in [[English language|English]], including ''flowering plum'' or ''plum blossoms''. Another misnomer, ''Japanese apricot'', likely derives from the plant's introduction into Western knowledge by [[Philipp Franz von Siebold]], who encountered it while living in Japan. 

The flower is known as the ''meihua'' ({{lang|zh|梅花}}) in Chinese, which came to be translated as "plum blossom"<ref name="kilpatrick-jane">{{cite book|last=Kilpatrick|first=Jane|title=Gifts from the Gardens of China|year=2007|publisher=[[Frances Lincoln Ltd]]|location=London|isbn=978-0-7112-2630-2|pages=16–17|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dgsfa13J2OIC}}</ref> or sometimes as "flowering plum".<ref name="welch"/> The term "winter plum" may be used too, specifically with regard to the depiction of the flower with its early blooming in [[Chinese painting]].{{cn|date=March 2023}} The character 梅 is a phono-semantic compound created by combining the semantic component {{linktext|木}} ("tree") with the phonetic component {{linktext|每}} (literally meaning "every," pronounced {{IPA|/*mɯːʔ/}} in [[Old Chinese]], which was similar to {{IPA|/*mɯː/}} for "plum").

In [[Chinese language|Chinese]], it is called ''mei'' ([[wikt:梅|梅]]) and the fruit is called ''meizi'' ([[wikt:梅子|梅子]]). The [[Japanese language|Japanese]] name is ''ume'' ([[wikt:うめ|うめ]]), while the [[Korean language|Korean]] name is ''maesil'' ({{Korean|hangul=[[wikt:매실|매실]]|hanja=[[wikt:梅實|梅實]]}}). The Japanese and Korean terms derive from [[Middle Chinese]], in which the pronunciation is thought to have been ''muəi''.<ref>Yamaguchi, Y., ed.: "''Kurashi no kotoba: Gogen Jiten''", page 103. Kodansha, 1998</ref> The [[Vietnamese language|Vietnamese]] name is ''[[wikt:mai#Vietnamese|mai]]'' or ''[[wikt:mơ|mơ]]'' (although ''mai vàng'' refers to a different plant, ''[[Ochna integerrima]]'', in southern Vietnam).{{cn|date=March 2023}}

== Varieties ==
[[Ornamental tree]] varieties and cultivars of ''P. mume'' have been cultivated for planting in various [[East Asian gardens|gardens throughout East Asia]], and for cut blossoming branches used in flower arrangements.{{cn|date=March 2023}}

=== Chinese varieties ===
[[File:Phylogenetic tree and ten representative traits of 348 mei accessions.jpg|thumb|Phylogenetic tree and ten representative traits]]
In China, there are over 300 recorded [[cultivar]]s of ''Prunus mume''.<ref name=cas>{{cite web|title=梅和梅的品种|url=http://www.kepu.cn/gb/lives/plantae/html/75.htm|work=Science Museums of China|publisher=[[Chinese Academy of Sciences]]|access-date=28 August 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241126204419/http://www.kepu.net.cn/gb/lives/plantae/html/75.htm |archive-date=26 November 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref> These are classified by their [[phylogenetic]]s (''P. mume'' and hybrids) into branches, characteristics of their branches in groups, and characteristics of their flowers in forms:<ref name=cas/>
* Upright Mei Group ({{lang|zh|直枝梅類}}), ''Prunus mume'' var. ''typica''
** Pleiocarpa Form ({{lang|zh|品字梅型}})
** Single Flowered Form ({{lang|zh|江梅型}})
** Pink Double Form ({{lang|zh|宮粉型}})
** Alboplena Form ({{lang|zh|玉蝶型}})
** Flavescens Form ({{lang|zh|黃香型}})
** Green Calyx Form ({{lang|zh|綠萼型}})
** Versicolor Form ({{lang|zh|灑金型}}) 
** Cinnabar Purple Form ({{lang|zh|硃砂型}})
* Pendulous Mei Group ({{lang|zh|垂枝梅類}}), ''Prunus mume'' var. ''pendula''
** Pink Pendulous Form ({{lang|zh|粉花垂枝型}})
** Versicolor Pendulous Form ({{lang|zh|五寶垂枝型}})
** Albiflora Pendulous Form ({{lang|zh|殘雪垂枝型}})
** Viridiflora Pendulous Form ({{lang|zh|白碧垂枝型}})
** Atropurpurea Pendulous Form ({{lang|zh|骨紅垂枝型}})
* Tortuous Dragon Group ({{lang|zh|龍游梅類}}), ''Prunus mume'' var. ''tortuosa''
* Apricot Mei Group ({{lang|zh|杏梅類}}), ''Prunus mume'' var. ''bungo''
* Blireiana Group ({{lang|zh|櫻李梅類}}), ''[[Prunus × blireana]], Prunus cerasifera 'Pissardii' × Prunus mume Alphandii''

It is disputed whether ''Prunus zhengheensis'' ({{zh|政和杏}}) is a separate species<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Tong |first1=Yihua |last2=Xia |first2=Nianhe |date=2016 |title=New combinations of Rosaceae, Urticaceae and Fagaceae from China |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/305115963 |journal=Biodiversity Science |volume=24 |issue=6 |pages=714–718 |doi=10.17520/biods.2016071 |access-date=18 September 2018|doi-access=free }}</ref> or conspecific with ''Prunus mume''.<ref>{{cite journal |author=王家琼 |author2=王家琼 |author3=吴保欢 |author4=崔大方 |author5=羊海军 |author6=黄峥 |author7=齐安民 |date=14 November 2016 |script-title=zh:基于30个形态性状的中国杏属（Armeniaca Scop.）植物分类学研究 |trans-title=Taxonomic study on ''Armeniaca'' Scop. species in China based on thirty morphological characters |url=http://www.airitilibrary.com/Publication/alDetailedMesh?docid=zwzyyhjxb201603017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180918123659/http://www.airitilibrary.com/Publication/alDetailedMesh?docid=zwzyyhjxb201603017 |archive-date=2018-09-18 |script-journal=zh:植物资源与环境学报 |volume=2016 |issue=3 |pages=103–111 |access-date=18 September 2018}}</ref> It is found in the Fujian province of China. It is only known from one county, [[Zhenghe County|Zhenghe]]. It is a tree that prefers to grow at {{cvt|700|-|1000|m}} above sea level. The yellow fruit is delectable and aside from its height, it is indistinguishable from ''P. mume''.

=== Japanese varieties ===
In Japan, [[Ornamental plant|ornamental]] ''Prunus mume'' [[cultivar]]s are classified into ''yabai'' (wild), ''hibai'' (red), and ''bungo'' ([[Bungo Province]]) types. The ''bungo'' trees are also grown for fruit and are hybrids between ''Prunus mume'' and apricot. The ''hibai'' trees have red [[Wood#Heartwood and sapwood|heartwood]] and most of them have red flowers. The ''yabai'' trees are also used as [[grafting]] stock. Among yabai trees, Nankoume is a very popular variety in Japan,<ref>{{Cite web|title=日本国政府農林水産省近畿農政局農林水産統計|url=https://www.maff.go.jp/kinki/toukei/toukeikikaku/yotei/attach/pdf/2018-26.pdf}}</ref> and whose fruits are mainly used for making ''[[umeboshi]]''.

In China, ''[[suanmeitang]]'' ({{lang|zh-hant|酸梅湯}}; "sour plum juice") is made from [[smoked plum]]s, called ''wumei'' ({{lang|zh-hant|烏梅}}).<ref name=leung>{{cite book|last=Khan|first=Ikhlas A.|title=Leung's encyclopedia of common natural ingredients: used in food, drugs, and cosmetics|year=2008|publisher=Wiley|location=Hoboken, N.J.|isbn=978-0-471-46743-4|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=z8rZzaHOrZsC|edition=3rd|author2=Abourashed, Ehab A. }}</ref> The plum juice is extracted by boiling smoked plums in water and sweetened with sugar to make ''suanmeitang''.<ref name=leung/> It ranges from light pinkish-orange to purplish black in colour and often has a smoky and slightly salty taste. It is traditionally flavoured with [[sweet osmanthus]] flowers, and is enjoyed chilled, usually in summer.{{cn|date=December 2023}}

In Korea, both the flowers and the fruits are used to make tea. ''[[Maehwa-cha]]'' ({{lang|ko|매화차, 梅花茶}}; "plum blossom tea") is made by infusing the flowers in hot water. ''[[Maesil-cha]]'' ({{lang|ko|매실차, 梅實茶}}; "plum tea") is made by mixing water with ''[[maesil-cheong]]'' (plum syrup) and is served either hot or cold.{{cn|date=December 2023}}

In Japan, a similar drink is made from green plums and tastes sweet and tangy, is considered a cold, refreshing drink, and is often enjoyed in the summer.{{cn|date=December 2023}}

A thick, sweet Chinese sauce called ''meijiang'' ({{lang|zh-hant|梅醬}}) or ''meizijiang'' ({{lang|zh-hant|梅子醬}}), usually translated as "[[plum sauce]]", is also made from the plums,<ref name="kilpatrick-jane"/> along with other ingredients such as sugar, vinegar, salt, ginger, chili, and garlic.  Similar to [[duck sauce]], it is used as a [[condiment]] for various Chinese dishes, including poultry dishes and [[egg roll]]s.{{cn|date=December 2023}}

In Korea, ''[[maesil-cheong]]'' ({{lang|ko|매실청, 梅實淸}}, "plum syrup"), a syrup made by [[sugaring]] ripe plums, is used as a [[condiment]] and [[sugar substitute]]. It can be made by simply mixing plums and [[sugar]] together, and then leaving them for about 100 days.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news|url=https://koreajoongangdaily.joins.com/news/article/article.aspx?aid=3017901|title=A taste of Korea with three regional delights|last=Baek|first=Jong-hyun|date=23 April 2016|newspaper=[[JoongAng Ilbo|Korea JoongAng Daily]]|access-date=17 December 2016}}</ref> To make syrup, the ratio of sugar to plum should be at least 1:1 to prevent [[fermentation]], by which the liquid may turn into [[plum wine]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://news.khan.co.kr/kh_news/khan_art_view.html?artid=201606011806422|title=청(淸)과 발효액은 어떻게 다를까?|last=Han|first=Dongha|date=1 June 2016|newspaper=[[Kyunghyang Shinmun]]|language=ko|trans-title=What's the difference between cheong(syrup) and fermented liquor?|access-date=18 December 2016}}</ref> The plums can be removed after 100 days, and the syrup can be consumed right away, or mature for a year or more.<ref name=":0" />

==== Flower pancake ====
[[File:Maehwajeon.jpg|150px|thumb|''[[Maehwa-jeon]]'']]
In Korea, ''[[hwajeon]]'' ({{lang|ko|화전, 花煎}}; "flower pancake") can be made with plum blossoms. Called ''[[maehwa-jeon]]'' ({{lang|ko|매화전, 梅花煎}}; "plum blossom pancake"), the pancake dish is usually sweet, with honey as an ingredient.{{cn|date=December 2023}}

Plum liquor, also known as [[plum wine]], is popular in both Japan and Korea, and is also produced in China. ''[[Umeshu]]'' ({{lang|ja|梅酒}}; "plum wine") is a Japanese alcoholic drink made by steeping green plums in [[shōchū]] (clear liquor). It is sweet and smooth. A similar liquor in Korea, called ''[[maesil-ju]]'' ({{lang|ko|매실주, 梅實酒}}; "plum wine"), is marketed under various brand names, including Mae hwa soo, Matchsoon, and Seoljungmae.  Both the Japanese and Korean varieties of plum liquor are available with whole plum fruits contained in the bottle. In China, plum wine is called ''méijiǔ'' ({{lang|zh|梅酒}}).{{cn|date=December 2023}}

In [[Taiwan]], a popular 1950s innovation over the Japanese-style plum wine is the ''wumeijiu'' ({{lang|zh|烏梅酒}}; "smoked plum liquor"), which is made by mixing two types of plum liquor, ''meijiu'' ({{lang|zh|梅酒}}) made of ''P. mume'' and ''lijiu'' ({{lang|zh|李酒}}), made of ''[[Prunus salicina|P. salicina]]'', and [[oolong]] tea liquor.<ref>Taiwan Tobacco and Liquor Corporation - Department of Liquor [http://liquor.ttl.com.tw/07products/products_view.aspx?sn=2384 烏梅酒] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080120234755/http://liquor.ttl.com.tw/07products/products_view.aspx?sn=2384 |date=2008-01-20 }}</ref>

In Vietnam, ripe plums are macerated in sticky rice liquor. The resulting liquor is called ''{{lang|vi|[[rượu mơ]]}}''.

In Chinese cuisine, plums pickled with vinegar and salt are called ''[[suanmeizi]]'' ({{lang|zh|酸梅子}}; "sour plum fruits"), and have an intensely sour and salty flavour. They are generally made from unripe plum fruits. ''[[Li hing mui|Huamei]]'' ({{lang|zh-hant|話梅}}) are Chinese preserved plums and refer to Chinese plums pickled in sugar, salt, and herbs. There are two general varieties: a dried variety, and a wet (pickled) variety.{{cn|date=December 2023}}

''[[Umeboshi]]'' ({{lang|ja|梅干}}) are pickled and dried plums. They are a Japanese specialty. Pickled with coarse salt, they are quite salty and sour, and therefore eaten sparingly. They are often red in colour when purple [[shiso]] leaves are used.  Plums used for making ''umeboshi'' are harvested in late May or early June, while they are ripe enough in yellow, and layered with much salt.<ref>{{Cite web|title=昔ながらの保存食！梅干し：農林水産省|url=https://www.maff.go.jp/j/zyukyu/foodstock/imadoki/imadoki07.html|website=www.maff.go.jp|access-date=2020-05-30}}</ref>  They are weighed down with a heavy stone (or some more modern implement) until late August.  They are then dried in the sun on bamboo mats for several days (they are returned to the salt at night). The [[flavonoid]] pigment in shiso leaves gives them their distinctive colour and a richer flavour. ''Umeboshi'' are generally eaten with rice as part of a [[bento]] (boxed lunch), although they may also be used in [[Sushi#Makizushi|makizushi]] (rolled sushi). ''Umeboshi'' are also used as a popular filling for [[Onigiri|rice ball]]s (onigiri) wrapped in [[nori]]. Makizushi made with plums may be made with either ''umeboshi'' or ''bainiku'' (''umeboshi'' paste), often in conjunction with green shiso leaves. A byproduct of ''umeboshi'' production is ''umeboshi'' vinegar, a salty, sour condiment.{{cn|date=December 2023}}

In Korea, there is 'maesil-jangajji' which is similar to 'umeboshi'. It is a common side dish in Korea.{{cn|date=December 2023}}

A very similar variety of pickled plum, ''{{lang|vi|xí muội}}'' or ''{{lang|vi|ô mai}}'' is used in [[Vietnamese cuisine]]. The best fruit for this are from the forest around the [[Perfume Pagoda|Hương Pagoda]] in [[Hà Tây Province]].

=== Traditional medicine ===
''Prunus mume'' is a common fruit in Asia and is used in [[traditional Chinese medicine]].<ref>{{cite book|last=Liu|first=Zhanwen|title=Essentials of Chinese medicine|year=2009|publisher=Springer|location=New York|isbn=978-1-84882-111-8|page=273|author2=Liu, Liang}}</ref>

== Cultural significance ==
Plum blossoms have been well-loved and celebrated across the East Asian cultural sphere, beginning in China and later introduced to  Vietnam, Korea, and Japan.

[[File:Manual of Plum Blossom Painting.jpg|thumbnail|Manual of Plum Blossom Painting, by Song Dynasty painter Song Boren]]
The plum blossom, which is known as the ''meihua'' ({{lang|zh|梅花}}), is one of the most beloved flowers in China and has been frequently depicted in Chinese art and poetry for centuries.<ref name="welch"/> The plum blossom is seen as a symbol of winter and a harbinger of spring.<ref name="welch"/> The blossoms are so beloved because they are viewed as blooming most vibrantly amidst the winter snow, exuding an ethereal elegance,<ref name="welch"/><ref name=npm-intro>{{cite web|title=The Three Friends of Winter: Paintings of Pine, Plum, and Bamboo from the Museum Collection (Introduction)|url=http://www.npm.gov.tw/exh91/3friends/english/infor.htm|publisher=National Palace Museum|access-date=10 August 2011|date=January 2003}}</ref> while their fragrance is noticed to still subtly pervade the air at even the coldest times of the year.<ref name=npm-intro/><ref name=caizq/> Therefore, the plum blossom came to symbolize perseverance and hope, as well as beauty, purity, and the transitoriness of life.<ref name="welch"/> In [[Confucianism]], the plum blossom stands for the principles and values of virtue.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Bartók|first1=Mira|last2=Ronan|first2=Christine|title=Ancient China|year=1994|publisher=Good Year Books|isbn=978-0-673-36180-6|page=13|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6hSIQpK4myMC}}</ref> More recently, it has also been used as a metaphor to symbolize revolutionary struggle since the turn of the 20th century.<ref>{{cite book|last=Ip|first=Hung-yok|title=Intellectuals in revolutionary China, 1921-1949: leaders, heroes and sophisticates|year=2005|publisher=Routledge|location=Oxfordshire|isbn=978-0-415-35165-2|pages=103, 110|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Eazcy0Zrt7QC}}</ref>

Because it blossoms in the cold winter, the plum blossom is regarded as one of the "[[Three Friends of Winter]]", along with pine, and bamboo.<ref name="kilpatrick-jane"/><ref name="heinrich-sally"/> The plum blossom is also regarded as one of the "[[Four Gentlemen]]" of flowers in Chinese art, together with the orchid, chrysanthemum, and bamboo.<ref name="heinrich-sally">{{cite book|last=Heinrich|first=Sally|title=Key into China|year=2007|publisher=Curriculum Press|isbn=978-1-86366-697-8|pages=28, 80|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=GchvhEH7BHIC}}</ref> It is one of the "Flowers of the Four Seasons", which consist of the orchid (spring), the lotus (summer), the chrysanthemum (autumn) and the plum blossom (winter).<ref name="heinrich-sally"/> These groupings are seen repeatedly in the Chinese aesthetic of art, painting, literature, and garden design.<ref name=forsyth>{{cite book|last=Forsyth|first=Holly|title=Gardens of Eden: Among the World's Most Beautiful Gardens|year=2010|publisher=The Miegunyah Press|page=104|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=I62swaaPP3oC|isbn=978-0-522-85776-4}}</ref>

An example of the plum blossom's literary significance is found in the life and work of poet [[Lin Bu]] ({{lang|zh|林逋}}) of the [[Song dynasty]] (960–1279). For much of his later life, Lin Bu lived in quiet reclusion on a cottage by [[West Lake]] in [[Hangzhou]], China.<ref>{{cite book|last=Fong|first=Grace S.|title=Herself an author: gender, agency, and writing in late Imperial China|year=2008|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-3186-8|page=58|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CWBRWV8Zug0C}}</ref> According to stories, he loved plum blossoms and cranes so much that he considered the plum blossom of Solitary Hill at West Lake as his wife and the cranes of the lake as his children, thus he could live peacefully in solitude.<ref>China Travel Guide. [https://www.travelchinaguide.com/attraction/zhejiang/hangzhou/solitary.htm "Gu Shan (Solitary Hill)"]. Retrieved 9 August 2011.</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Schmidt|first=Jerry Dean|title=Harmony Garden: the life, literary criticism, and poetry of Yuan Mei (1716-1799)|year=2003|publisher=Routledge|location=London|isbn=978-0-7007-1525-1|page=641|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nB1feh4lXw4C}}</ref> One of his most famous poems is "Little Plum Blossom of Hill Garden" ({{lang|zh|山園小梅}}). The Chinese text, as well as a translation, follows:<ref>Red Pine. Poems of the Masters. Port Townsend, Copper Canyon Press, 2003, p. 453.</ref>
{{verse translation|lang=zh|italicsoff=yes|
眾芳搖落獨暄妍，
占斷風情向小園。
疏影橫斜水清淺，
暗香浮動月黃昏。
霜禽欲下先偷眼，
粉蝶如知合斷魂。
幸有微吟可相狎，
不須檀板共金樽。
|
When everything has faded they alone shine forth,
encroaching on the charms of smaller gardens.
Their scattered shadows fall lightly on clear water,
their subtle scent pervades the moonlit dusk.
Snowbirds look again before they land,
butterflies would faint if they but knew.
Thankfully, I can flirt in whispered verse,
I don't need a sounding board or winecup.
}}

As with the literary culture amongst the educated of the time, Lin Bu's poems were discussed in several Song dynasty era commentaries on poetry. Wang Junqing remarked after quoting the third and fourth line: "''This is from Lin Hejing's [Lin Bu's] plum blossom poem. Yet these lines might just as well be applied to the flowering apricot, peach, or pear.''"—a comparison of the flowers with the plum blossom to which the renowned Song dynasty poet [[Su Dongpo]]<!-- also known as Su Shi or Su Zizhan --> ({{lang|zh|蘇東坡}}) replied, "''Well, yes, they might. But I'm afraid the flowers of those other trees wouldn't presume to accept such praise.''"<ref name=caizq>{{cite book|last=Cai|first=Zong-qi|title=How to read Chinese poetry: A guided anthology|year=2008|publisher=Columbia University Press|location=New York|isbn=978-0-231-13941-0|pages=210–311|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=h8fWf7pYOIUC}}</ref> Plum blossoms inspired many people of the era.<ref name=dudbridge>{{cite book|last=Dudbridge|first=Glen|title=Reading China|year=2007|publisher=Brill|location=Leiden|isbn=978-90-04-15483-4|pages=56–58|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rPwu3MsCebcC|author2=Berg, Daria }}</ref>
[[File:畫麗珠萃秀 Gathering Gems of Beauty (宋壽陽公主) 2.jpg|thumb|Princess Shouyang, who is prominently featured in a Chinese legend about plum blossoms]]
Legend has it that once on the 7th day of the 1st lunar month, while Princess Shouyang ({{lang|zh|壽陽公主}}), daughter of [[Emperor Wu of Liu Song]] ({{lang|zh|劉宋武帝}}), was resting under the eaves of Hanzhang Palace near the plum trees after wandering in the gardens, a plum blossom drifted down onto her fair face, leaving a floral imprint on her forehead that enhanced her beauty further.<ref name=cai>{{cite book|title=How to read Chinese poetry: A guided anthology|year=2008|publisher=Columbia University Press|location=New York|isbn=978-0-231-13941-0|page=295|editor=Cai, Zong-qi|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=h8fWf7pYOIUC&pg=PA295}}</ref><ref name=bettyw>{{cite web|last=Wang|first=Betty|title=Flower deities mark the lunar months with stories of Love & Tragedy|url=http://taiwanreview.nat.gov.tw/ct.asp?xItem=115157&CtNode=1900|work=Taiwan Review|publisher=Government Information Office, Republic of China|access-date=20 November 2011 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120525043800/http://taiwanreview.nat.gov.tw/ct.asp?xItem=115157&CtNode=1900 | archive-date= 25 May 2012}}</ref><ref name=w&e>{{cite journal|journal=West & East 中美月刊|year=1991|volume=36-37|page=9|title=Taiwan periodicals_West & East|url=https://books.google.com/books?ei=qXyQTqOYOIqVOpbimcwN|issn=0043-3047}}</ref> The court ladies were said to be so impressed that they started decorating their own foreheads with a small delicate plum blossom design.<ref name=cai/><ref name=bettyw/><ref name=chinat/> This is also the mythical origin of the floral fashion, ''[[Huadian (make-up)|meihua chuang]]''<ref name=bettyw/><!-- "mei hua chuang" in ref --> (梅花妝; literally "plum blossom makeup"), that originated in the [[Southern Dynasties]] (420–589) and became popular amongst ladies in the [[Tang dynasty|Tang]] (618–907) and [[Song dynasty|Song]] (960–1279) dynasties.<ref name=chinat>{{cite web|last=Huo|first=Jianying|title=Ancient Cosmetology|url=http://www.chinatoday.com.cn/English/e2004/e200411/p60.htm|publisher=China Today|access-date=8 October 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120509163143/http://www.chinatoday.com.cn/English/e2004/e200411/p60.htm|archive-date=9 May 2012}}</ref><ref name=huamei>{{cite book|last=Mei|first=Hua|title=Chinese clothing|year=2011|publisher=Cambridge University Press|location=Cambridge|isbn=978-0-521-18689-6|page=32|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ayKNyCz0cOEC|quote=For example, the Huadian or forehead decoration was said to have originated in the South Dynasty, when the Shouyang Princess was taking a walk in the palace in early spring and a light breeze brought a plum blossom onto her forehead. The plum blossom for some reason could not be washed off or removed in any way. Fortunately, it looked beautiful on her, and all of a sudden became all the rage among the girls of the commoners. It is therefore called the "Shouyang makeup" or the "plum blossom makeup." This makeup was popular among women for a long time in the Tang and Song Dynasties.}}</ref> The markings of plum blossom designs on the foreheads of court ladies were usually made with paintlike materials such as [[sorghum]] powder, [[gold]] powder, [[paper]], [[jade]], and other tint substances. Princess Shouyang is celebrated as the goddess of the plum blossom in Chinese culture.<ref name=bettyw/><ref name=w&e/>

During the [[Ming dynasty]] (1368–1644), the garden designer [[Ji Cheng (Ming dynasty)|Ji Cheng]] wrote his definitive garden architecture monograph ''[[The Craft of Gardens|Yuanye]]'' and in it, he described the plum tree as the "beautiful woman of the forest and moon".<ref name=dudbridge/> The appreciation of nature at night plays an important role in [[Chinese gardens]]. For this reason, there are classical pavilions for the tradition of viewing plum blossoms by the moonlight.<ref>{{cite book|last=Thacker|first=Christopher|title=The history of gardens|year=1985|publisher=University of California Press|location=Berkeley|isbn=978-0-520-05629-9|page=[https://archive.org/details/historyofgardens00chri/page/57 57]|url=https://archive.org/details/historyofgardens00chri|url-access=registration}}</ref> The flowers are viewed and enjoyed by many as annual plum blossom festivals take place in the blooming seasons of the ''meihua''. The festivals take place throughout China (for example, [[West Lake]] in [[Hangzhou]] and scenic spots near [[Zijin Mountain]] in [[Nanjing]], amongst other places).<ref>[http://www.china.org.cn/video/2010-02/24/content_19467998.htm Int'l Plum Blossom Festival draws crowds in Nanjing]. Retrieved 9 August 2011.</ref><ref>{{cite to display the blossoms in a home since the early [[Song dynasty]] (960–1279).<ref>{{cite web|title=meiping|url=http://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/373257/meiping|publisher=Encyclopædia The [[Moy Yat]] lineage of [[Wing Chun]] [[kung fu]] uses a red plum flower blossom as its symbol. The plum blossoms are featured on one of the four flowers that appear on [[mahjong tile set]]s, where ''mei'' ({{lang|zh|梅}}) is usually simply translated as "plum" in English.<ref>{{cite book|last=Lo|first=Amy|title=The book of mahjong: An illustrated guide|year=2001|publisher=Tuttle Publishing|location=Boston|isbn=978-0-8048-3302-8|pages=[https://archive.org/details/bookofmahjongill00loam/page/47 47–48]|url=https://archive.org/details/bookofmahjongill00loam/page/47}}</ref>

It has been suggested that the Japanese practice of ''hanami'' may have originated from the [[China|Chinese]] custom of enjoying poetry and wine underneath plum blossom trees while viewing their flowers, that was replicated by Japanese elites. This is supported by the fact that ''hanami'' started in urban areas rather than rural areas, that Japanese people initially admired plum blossoms like the Chinese rather than cherry blossoms, and that classic Japanese poetry does not associate [[Cherry blossom|cherry blossoms]] with merriness.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hannes Palang |title=Seasonal Landscapes Volume 7 of Landscape Series |last2=Helen Sooväli |last3=Anu Printsmann |date=2007 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-1-4020-4990-3 |page=223}}</ref>

In Korea, the plum blossom is a symbol for spring.<ref>{{cite book|last=Mullany|first=Francis|title=Symbolism in Korean ink brush painting|year=2006|publisher=Global Oriental|location=Folkestone|isbn=978-1-901903-89-8|page=18|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vc3qAAAAMAAJ}}</ref>  It is a popular flower motif, amongst other flowers, for [[Korean embroidery]].<ref>{{cite book|last=Lee|first=Kyung-ja|title=Traditional Korean costume|year=2007|publisher=Global Oriental|location=Folkestone, Kent, UK|isbn=978-1-905246-04-5|page=125|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5unfAAAAMAAJ |author2=Hong, Na-young |author3=Chang, Sook-hwan }}</ref> Maebyong are plum vases derived from the Chinese meiping and are traditionally used to hold branches of plum blossoms in Korea.<ref>{{cite web|title=Vase (Maebyeong) with Lotus Blossoms|url=https://www.philamuseum.org/collections/permanent/69248.html|publisher=Philadelphia Museum of Art|access-date=22 August 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Smith|first=Judith G.|title=Arts of Korea|year=1998|publisher=Metropolitan Museum of Art|location=New York|isbn=978-0-87099-850-8|page=415|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pgTqAAAAMAAJ&q=maebyong+meiping}}</ref> Korean [[Ceramic art|ceramist]] Master [[Kim Se-yong (ceramist)|Kim Se-yong]] incorporates the blossom into many of his [[openwork]] [[celadon]] vases.

Also, during [[Korean Empire]] period, the plum blossom became [[Imperial Seal of Korea|the imperial seal]] and royal official flower. Since ancient times, plum blossom has been filled with meaning and mystery. Plum blossoms bloom at the end of the winter, and because of this, they are called the herald of spring. They also symbolize perseverance because of how they can possibly bloom during the cold winter. Since they are considered the first flower of the year, they also represent purity and renewal. Plum flowers have five petals which are believed to carry 5 different blessings such as: wealth, health, virtue, peaceful and natural death.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Plum Blossoms, its Symbolism and Meanings |url=https://www.lotusfun.com/blogs/lotusfun/plum-blossoms-its-symbolism-and-meanings |access-date=2023-05-19 |website=Lotus Fun |language=en}}</ref>

==== Japanese ====
Plum blossoms are often mentioned in [[Japanese poetry]] as a symbol of spring, as well as elegance and purity. When used in [[haiku]] or [[renga]], they are a ''[[kigo]]'' or season word for early spring. The blossoms are associated with the [[Japanese bush warbler]] and are depicted together on one of the twelve [[Suit (cards)|suits]] of [[hanafuda]] (Japanese playing cards).<ref>{{cite book|last=Nakamura|first=Shigeki|title=Pattern sourcebook: Nature 2: 250 patterns for projects and designs|year=2009|publisher=Rockport Publishing|location=Beverly, Mass.|isbn=978-1-59253-559-0|edition=1. publ.}}</ref> Plum blossoms were favored during the [[Nara period]] (710–794) until the emergence of the [[Heian period]] (794–1185), in which the cherry blossom was preferred.<ref>{{cite book|last=Parker|first=Mary S.|title=Sashiko: Easy & elegant Japanese designs for decorative machine embroidery|year=1999|publisher=Lark Books|location=Asheville, N.C.|isbn=978-1-57990-132-5|page=132}}</ref>

Japanese tradition holds that the ''ume'' functions as a protective charm against evil, so the ''ume'' is traditionally planted in the northeast of the garden, the direction from which evil is believed to come. The eating of the pickled fruit for breakfast is also supposed to stave off misfortune.<ref name=lp>Rowthorn, Chris and Florence, Mason. ''Lonely Planet:  Kyoto''. 2001, page 21.</ref>

The tradition of [[hanami]] was originally performed with plum blossoms rather than [[Cherry blossom|cherry blossoms]] as is common today. The specific custom of viewing plum blossoms in Japan is now called ''umemi'' (梅見, plum-viewing).<ref>{{Cite web |title=「梅見月」って何月のこと？梅から始まる江戸の花見を、美しい錦絵とともに紹介！ ｜ 和樂web 美の国ニッポンをもっと知る！ |url=https://intojapanwaraku.com/rock/culture-rock/143837/ |access-date=2024-02-21 |website=和樂web 美の国ニッポンをもっと知る！ |language=ja}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=梅見月 うめみづき｜暦生活 |url=https://www.543life.com/koyomi/post20230201.html |access-date=2024-02-21 |website=暦生活 |language=ja}}</ref>

=== Southeast Asia ===
==== Vietnamese ====
In [[Vietnam]], due to the beauty of the tree and its flowers, the word ''mai'' is used to name girls. The largest hospital in Hanoi is named [[Bạch Mai Hospital|Bạch Mai]] (white plum blossom),<ref>{{cite web|title=Bach Mai - Trang chủ|url=http://bachmaihospital.org/|publisher=Bach Mai Hospital|access-date=27 August 2011}}</ref> another hospital in Hanoi is named [[Mai Hương Hospital|Mai Hương]] ("the scent of plum"), situated in Hồng Mai (pink plum blossom) street.<ref>{{cite web|title=Mai Huong Hospital|url=http://www.maihuong.gov.vn/Default.asp?mnz=39&mno=0&Languageid=1|publisher=Mai Huong Day Psychiatric Hospital|access-date=27 August 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110726163905/http://www.maihuong.gov.vn/Default.asp?mnz=39&mno=0&Languageid=1|archive-date=26 July 2011}}</ref> [[Hoàng Mai District|Hoàng Mai]] (yellow plum blossom) is the name of a district in [[Hanoi]]. Bạch Mai is also a long and old street in Hanoi. All these places are located in the south part of Hanoi, where, in the past, many ''P. mume'' trees were grown.{{cn|date=December 2023}}
